In line with the input received and captured in Section 2, and the online session held on this AI, the discussion rapporteur proposes the following: Agree R2-2009748 (miscellaneous corrections, co-sourced by the BAP spec rapporteur), with the following editorial changes: Remove unaffected sections from the CR altogether (Section 2, 6) Add missing clauses to the list of affected clauses in the CR’s cover sheet (Clause 5.3.1, 5.4.1) Agree the following change to the NOTE in section 5.2.1.1, and merge with the revised CR from Proposal 1: NOTE: Data buffering on the transmitting part of the BAP entity, e.g., until RLC-AM entity has received an acknowledgement, is up to implementation. In case of BH RLF, the transmitting part of the BAP entity may reroute the BAP Data PDUs, which has not been acknowledged by lower layer before the BH RLF, to an alternative path whose BAP address matches the DESTINATION field.

{"chunk_id":"R2-2501248-006","collection":"ran2_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Ericsson"],"tdocNumber":"R2-2501248","title":"Improvements to specification handling"},"point_id":"2878253990572798121"}
aft the actual change, the delegate creates a new branch in Git(lab). Subsequently, the delegate implements the required changes in one or more affected files. When considered ready, the modifications are pushed to the Git(lab) server. It should be noted that the Git branch does not contain a complete CR as known from the traditional workflow. The branch contains the “CR body” (i.e. the change), only. Tied to the branch, a merge request is created. The merge requests contains the metadata (i.e. the cover page) such as reason for the proposed change and a summary of the change as well as pre-defined labels describing work item, CR type, and source working group. Some parameters that were mentioned explicitly in the traditional CR cover page can be derived directly from the version control system (e.g. the affected specification, the affected clauses of the specification, ...). The Gitlab platform allows filtering pending merge requests (= submitted CRs) by those properties and to preview the proposed changes directly in the web interface. The following screenshot shows a merge request in RAN4’s test repository on 3GPP’s Gitlab instance: Once a merge request has been created, it can be discussed in the RAN2 meeting. RAN2 typically has a high-level discussion of a CR on the floor in the RAN2 meeting, sometimes followed by more detailed discussions over email or in Word-bubbles. For those more detailed discussions, delegates may instead use the web interface to provide comments to the entire merge request (e.g. on the reason for change) or to specific changes in the affected clauses. Gitlab supports the latter in a user-friendly side-by-side diff-view of the current specification and the proposed changes: The author of the CR should, based on those comments, update the changes in the branch. These revisions are stored in the same branch and remain associated with the same merge request, i.e. are traceable. Thereby the merge requests will greatly simplify what used to be done in in a mix of email- and offline discussions and via (draft) revisions of docx CRs. The discussions around CRs would also become easier to trace back (including comments and questions and the changes among the versions of the CR throughout the discussion). If RAN2 agrees a CR during the discussions at a WG meeting, the merge request should be tagged as “agreed” in Gitlab. Only upon final approval at TSG RAN an authorized person (e.g. MCC or WG chair) marks the merge request as “approved” in Gitlab. Only then it may be merged into the main branch. If no other CR affecting the same file(s) and section(s) had been merged before, this step requires no further manual work. Otherwise, Git(lab) informs about the collision and assists specification-rapporteurs and MCC in the necessary update. The necessary revisions remain also visible in the CR’s branch.

In this paper, we provide some of our thinkings on how the readability of RRC procedural text and ASN.1 can be potentially improved. Since the creation of the NR RRC spec and after 5 releases since its creation, the RRC spec has evolved to spec of 1700+ pages as of its v1900 version. With such long spec, we need to re-examine its readability and sustainability. During the past ASN1 reviews, our main focus has been on the corrections of the ASN1 part, but one issue that might fall through the cracks might be the RRC procedure text. For the current RRC procedure text, there are several extra-long chapters spanning multiple pages. Some examples are include the following Table1. Table1, The length of certain clauses in the current RRC procedure text Under these sections, often time we see extra-long UE procedure that when one comes across with a “if” condition, the “else if” can be located two/several pages away, which provides bad reading experience for the readers. From our point of view, one main reason for these extra-long sections is because during multiple releases, changes brought by different features are just added upon the old sections without any re-structuring. This makes a single RRC procedure to carry UE procedures for multiple features, only to be separated by the configuration condition in the procedure text. Without any proper structures, it is quite difficult for the readers to easily unpack the procedure text. Take the following paragraph in “Reception of RRCReconfiguration by the UE" as an example. UE procedures specified for configuration of appLayerMeasConfig is specified in detail in reception of RRCReconfiguration by the UE. This makes the main text of the clause Reception of RRCreconfiguration by the UE unnecessarily long and hard to read. Figure1, RRC procedure for the reception of RRCRecconfiguration with appLayerMeasConfig For this part of spec boxed in red, it is only applicable for appLayerIdleInactiveConfig. This procedure in the red box could be specified in a separate section only for the reception of appLayerMeasConfig included in RRCReconfiguration The following could be done for better readability: Based on the discussions above, we propose the following for enhancing the readability of RRC procedure text Proposal 1: For better readability of RRC procedure text, separate UE procedures belonging to different features within a long section to separate section for each feature. Take the TP in appendix A as an example. In the current R19 feature agreed CRs and some legacy RRC ASN.1 part, it is observed below examples: “BIT STRING (SIZE (x))” are used multiple times for different sub-fields, while the only difference is the size; “INTEGER(x..y)” are used multiple times for different sub-fields, while the only difference is the value range;

As mentioned in Section 1, it has been agreed that upon successful completion of contention resolution, the UE shall monitor C-RNTI, in particular to receive UL grants for subsequent transmissions. In a previous contribution [3] we discussed how for RA-SDT with subsequent data the contention could be resolved (a) immediately after Msg3/MsgA transmission through a DL transmission containing the Contention Resolution ID (CRID) or (b) at the end of the SDT procedure when the gNB sends a DL RRC message to either release the connection or move the UE in RRC_CONNECTED. Nevertheless, considering the agreement in Section 1, option (a) is the only one that allows the UE to use C-RNTI for the subsequent transmission scheduling. For this reason, it should be agreed that contention is resolved immediately after Msg3 or MsgA transmission. Although this is a legacy behaviour, it might not be clear that this behaviour is required also for SDT. Moreover, by resolving the contention immediately, the subsequent transmissions are not affected by collisions with other UEs, improving in general the performance of the system. There is no impact on 2-step RACH SDT, considering the general understanding of SDT before this discussion, as MsgB already contains the CRID in its legacy format. Also, differently from legacy, a DL RRC message is not needed, making MsgB smaller. The impact on 4-step RACH SDT is more relevant, because between Msg3 and the final RRC DL message the intention was to have only subsequent transmission in RRC_INACTIVE, but a short DL message containing the CRID is required after Msg3 transmission. Contention Resolution ID is sent (4-step RACH) in a DL transmission immediately after Msg3 (this transmission, differently from the legacy Msg4 will not contain DL RRC messages), or (2-step RACH) in MsgB. It is worth mentioning that based on the analysis of subsequent packet transmission presented in [3], adding one further DL transmission after Msg3 reduces even more the usefulness of sending multiple packet transmissions in RRC_INACTIVE rather than moving the UE to RRC_CONNECTED. The gain appears to be limited to the inclusion of data in Msg3 rather than on the subsequent packet transmissions. Sending the contention resolution ID after Msg3 in 4-step RACH SDT, reduces the usefulness of sending multiple subsequent transmissions with respect to what presented in a previous contribution [3].
